title: NTA UGC NET English Full Mock Test #03
subtitle: 100 Questions · 200 Marks · Post-2018 NTA Pattern · Zero Answer Bias (25 A/B/C/D) · Reading Comprehension (Q91-100)

items.title: Mock #03 · Q1
items.stem:
Match the following :
(Browning's poems) — (Type of Character)
I. Abt Vogler — 1. A Medieval Knight
II. Andrea del Sarto — 2. A Musician
III. Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came — 3. A Poet
IV. Cleon — 4. An Artist
The right combination according to the code is :
Codes : I II III IV
items.explanation: In Robert Browning's dramatic monologues, 'Abt Vogler' is spoken by an eighteenth-century German musician/organist (I-2), 'Andrea del Sarto' by a Renaissance painter/artist (II-4), 'Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came' by a medieval knight on a quest (III-1), and 'Cleon' by a classical Greek poet (IV-3).

items.title: Mock #03 · Q2
items.stem:
Who of the following was not a
contemporary of Wordsworth and
Coleridge ?
items.explanation: Algernon Charles Swinburne (1837–1909) was a late Victorian poet, whereas Robert Southey (1774–1843), Sir Walter Scott (1771–1832), and William Hazlitt (1778–1830) were direct Romantic-era contemporaries of William Wordsworth (1770–1850) and S. T. Coleridge (1772–1834).

items.title: Mock #03 · Q3
items.stem:
Choose the plays written by Lord Byron
A. Sardanapalus
B. Hellas
C. Cain
D. The Two Foscari: An Historical Tragedy
E. The Cenci
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Sardanapalus (A), Cain: A Mystery (C), and The Two Foscari: An Historical Tragedy (D) are closet dramas by Lord Byron published together in a single volume in December 1821. Hellas (1822) and The Cenci (1819) were written by Percy Bysshe Shelley.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q4
items.stem: Who among the following gave a happy ending to King Lear ?
items.explanation: In 1681, Restoration playwright and future Poet Laureate Nahum Tate rewrote Shakespeare's tragedy as The History of King Lear, omitting the Fool and giving the play a happy ending in which Lear regains his throne and Cordelia survives to marry Edgar.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q5
items.stem:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of their publication :
(A) Studies in the History of the Renaissance by Walter Pater
(B) The French Revolution by Thomas Carlyle
(C) Unto this Last by John Ruskin
(D) The Making of England by John Richard Green
(E) On the Origin of Species by Charles Robert Darwin
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The French Revolution (1837), Origin of Species (1859), Unto this Last (1860), Pater's Studies (1873) and Green's The Making of England (1881) give B, E, C, A, D.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q6
items.stem:
Listed below are some English plays across several centuries :

Twelfth Night, She Stoops to Conquer, The Importance of Being Earnest, Pygmalion and
Blithe Spirit.

What is common to them ?
options: All romantic comedies; love and laughter
All ideologically framed; class and gender
All problem plays; scheming and intrigue
items.explanation: Spanning the Elizabethan era to the twentieth century, Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, Goldsmith's She Stoops to Conquer, Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest, Shaw's Pygmalion, and Coward's Blithe Spirit are all celebrated comedies centred on love, courtship, and laughter.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q7
items.stem:
Given below are two statements :
Statement I: According to W. H. Auden, The Importance of Being Earnest is the purest example in English Literature of a 'Verbal Opera'.
Statement II: Oscar Wilde possessed profound insight into the range of the arts that in a combined form make theatre performance possible.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
items.explanation: In his 1963 essay 'An Improbable Life,' W. H. Auden praised Oscar Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest (1895) as the only pure 'verbal opera' in English, and Wilde's dramatic aesthetic combined music, visual design, and theatrical performance (Both Statement I and Statement II are true).

items.title: Mock #03 · Q8
items.stem: Who among the following has composed the lyrical drama Hellas?
items.explanation: Percy Bysshe Shelley composed the verse lyrical drama Hellas in 1821 (published 1822) at Pisa, modeled on Aeschylus's The Persians, to celebrate and raise support for the Greek War of Independence against the Ottoman Empire.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q9
items.stem:
John Osborne's play Look Back in Anger :
(A) Represented real confusions among real people of the 1950's
(B) Is more important as a cultural phenomenon than as work of literature
(C) Is about a provincial graduate of humble social background
(D) Is about the upper-class society of 1990's
(E) Is Victorian in its outlook
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: John Osborne's Look Back in Anger (1956) captured the disillusionment of 1950s post-war British youth (A), became a landmark cultural phenomenon launching the 'Angry Young Men' movement (B), and centers on Jimmy Porter, a provincial university graduate from a working-class background (C), matching Option 3: (A), (B) and (C) Only.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q10
items.stem: Which of the following novelists did not employ “Stream of Consciousness” technique?
items.explanation: Virginia Woolf (Mrs Dalloway), James Joyce (Ulysses), and Dorothy Richardson (Pilgrimage) are pioneering modernists who famously deployed the stream-of-consciousness technique to capture internal human consciousness. Graham Greene wrote realistic psychological novels and Catholic moral thrillers without utilizing stream of consciousness.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q11
items.meta: Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem:
Match the authors under List – I with the titles under List – II :
List – I
(I) Claude Levi-Strauss
(II) Jacques Derrida
(III) Northrop Frye
(IV) Michel Foucault

List – II
(1) Of Grammatology
(2) The Archaeology of Knowledge
(3) Structural Anthropology
(4) Anatomy of Criticism

Codes : (I) (II) (III) (IV)
items.explanation: Claude Lévi-Strauss wrote Structural Anthropology (3), Jacques Derrida wrote Of Grammatology (1), Northrop Frye wrote Anatomy of Criticism (4), and Michel Foucault wrote The Archaeology of Knowledge (2).

items.title: Mock #03 · Q12
items.stem: Which of the following observations are true about Beatrice Culleton's April Raintree ? I. It is a fictional account of the lives of two metis sisters growing up in Winnipeg. II. April has a darker complexion and identifies herself with Metis population. III. The two sisters have been removed from their parents home and placed with a series of foster families. IV. Cheryl has a lighter complexion and identifies herself with white population
items.explanation: Beatrice Culleton Mosionier's novel In Search of April Raintree (1983) recounts the lives of two Métis sisters growing up in Winnipeg (I) who are taken from their alcoholic parents and placed in separate foster homes (III). Lighter-skinned April tries to pass as white, while darker-skinned Cheryl proudly identifies with the Métis people.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q13
items.stem:
Which of the following works have been authored by Thomas Carlyle?
A. Chartism
B. Past and Present
C. The French Revolution
D. Suspiria de Profundis
E. The English Mail Coach
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Victorian historian and social critic Thomas Carlyle authored Chartism (1839, A), Past and Present (1843, B), and The French Revolution: A History (1837, C). Suspiria de Profundis (1845) and The English Mail-Coach (1849) were written by Thomas De Quincey.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q14
items.stem: Who made the remark: "Great literature is simply language charged with meaning to the utmost possible degree"?
items.explanation: Modernist poet and critic Ezra Pound made this famous definition in his treatise 'How to Read' (1929) and reiterated it in ABC of Reading (1934).

items.title: Mock #03 · Q15
items.stem:
Arrange the following works of Raymond Williams in the correct chronological order of their publication -
A. Keywords
B. Culture and Society
C. The Long Revolution
D. The Country and the City
E. Modern Tragedy
Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: The chronological order of Raymond Williams's major books is: Culture and Society (B, 1958), The Long Revolution (C, 1961), Modern Tragedy (E, 1966), The Country and the City (D, 1973), and Keywords (A, 1976), giving B, C, E, D, A.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q16
items.stem: Who is the author of A Literature of their Own?
items.explanation: American feminist critic Elaine Showalter authored A Literature of Their Own: British Women Novelists from Brontë to Lessing (1977), a foundational work of gynocriticism.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q17
items.stem:
Read the following statement and the reason given for it. Choose the right response.
Assertion (A) : Gulliver's Travels earned Jonathan Swift the bad name of being a misanthrope.
Reason (R) : Swift in the novel was neutral to the image of man.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation.
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation.
items.explanation: Jonathan Swift's fierce satire on human pride and corruption—especially in Book IV of Gulliver's Travels (1726), where humanity is depicted as bestial Yahoos—earned him a reputation for misanthropy (making A true), whereas Reason R is false because Swift was bitingly satirical rather than neutral toward human nature.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q18
items.stem:
In a 1817 review of Coleridge’s Biographia Literaria, Francis Jeffrey coined the term
‘Lake School of Poets’ rouping...
items.explanation: Francis Jeffrey, editor of the Edinburgh Review, coined the term 'Lake School of Poets' in his 1817 review of Coleridge's Biographia Literaria to group William Wordsworth, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, and Robert Southey, who resided in the Lake District.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q19
items.stem:
Which of the following poems are written by Alexander Pope?
A. The Dunciad
B. Moral Essays
C. Grongar Hill
D. Cooper's Hill
E. Absalom and Achitophel
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The Dunciad (1728-1743) (A) and Moral Essays (Epistles to Several Persons, 1731-1735) (B) were written by Alexander Pope. Grongar Hill (1726) is by John Dyer, Cooper's Hill (1642) is by Sir John Denham, and Absalom and Achitophel (1681) is by John Dryden.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q20
items.stem: Which of the following plays of Bernard Shaw attacks Darwinism?
items.explanation: In Back to Methuselah (1921), a five-part play cycle spanning from the Garden of Eden into the distant future, George Bernard Shaw explicitly attacks Darwinian natural selection as blind and mechanistic, championing Lamarckian creative evolution driven by the Life Force.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q21
items.stem:
Match List I with List IT

|Author Text

A. Michel de Certeau I. Distinction

B. John Fiske ll. Reading the Romance
Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: In cultural studies, Michel de Certeau wrote The Practice of Everyday Life (1980), and John Fiske authored Understanding Popular Culture (1989). Pierre Bourdieu published Distinction: A Social Critique of the Judgement of Taste (1979), and Janice Radway wrote the ethnographic reception study Reading the Romance (1984).

items.title: Mock #03 · Q22
items.stem: "Provincializing Europe" is a concept propounded by
items.explanation: Postcolonial historian and Subaltern Studies theorist Dipesh Chakrabarty propounded the concept in his landmark book Provincializing Europe: Postcolonial Thought and Historical Difference (2000), critiquing the treatment of European history as the universal norm of modernity.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q23
items.stem:
'A Valediction Forbidding Mourning' is written by
A. John Donne
B. John Milton
C. Adrienne Rich
D. Sylvia Plath
E. Robert Frost
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Both John Donne (A) and Adrienne Rich (C) wrote famous poems titled 'A Valediction Forbidding Mourning'. Donne's metaphysical lyric (written c. 1611, published 1633) uses the conceit of twin compasses, while Adrienne Rich's 1970 feminist poem reimagines parting and language.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q24
items.stem: Who among the following proposed that the English language is "man made", not 'woman made'?
items.explanation: Australian feminist scholar Dale Spender advanced this argument in her landmark book Man Made Language (1980), contending that in patriarchal societies men have historically controlled language, meanings, and linguistic norms.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q25
items.stem:
Arrange the following campus novels in the correct chronological order of their publication.
A. J.M. Coetzee's Disgrace
B. Malcolm Bradbury's The History Man
C. Mary McCarthy's The Groves of Academe
D. Evelyn Waugh's Brideshead Revisited
E. Philip Roth's The Human Stain
Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: The chronological order of these novels is: Evelyn Waugh's Brideshead Revisited (D, 1945), Mary McCarthy's The Groves of Academe (C, 1952), Malcolm Bradbury's The History Man (B, 1975), J. M. Coetzee's Disgrace (A, 1999), and Philip Roth's The Human Stain (E, 2000), giving D, C, B, A, E.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q26
items.stem: Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding is a classic statement of _________ Philosophy
items.explanation: John Locke's An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689) is the foundational statement of British Empiricist philosophy, rejecting the doctrine of innate ideas and arguing that the mind at birth is a tabula rasa (blank slate) shaped entirely by sensory experience and reflection.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q27
items.stem: Assertion (A) : The world is becoming increasingly multilingual. Reason (R) : To monolingual Anglophones it may look like everyone in the world is learning English. In the context of these two statements
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
items.explanation: Both statements are sociolinguistically true: global population growth and mobility expand multilingualism across the globe (A), and native English speakers frequently assume that worldwide learning of English equals universal adoption of English alone (R). However, (R) merely describes a monolingual Anglophone bias rather than providing the causal reason for global multilingual growth (A).

items.title: Mock #03 · Q28
items.stem:
William Blake's famous poems such
as "London", "The Sick Rose", and
"The Tyger" appear in
options: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
Vision of the Daughters of Albion J-30-12
items.explanation: 'London', 'The Sick Rose', and 'The Tyger' all appear in William Blake's Songs of Experience (1794), the darker, socially critical companion volume to his earlier Songs of Innocence (1789).

items.title: Mock #03 · Q29
items.stem:
Which two of the following were published in the year 1859?
(A) On the Origin of Species
(B) A Tale of Two Cities
(C) Alice in Wonderland
(D) Silas Marner
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: Darwin's On the Origin of Species and Dickens's A Tale of Two Cities appeared in 1859. Alice came in 1865 and Silas Marner in 1861.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q30
items.stem: Which one of the following essays holds that "As a method, realism is a complete failure"?
options: Virginia Woolf, "The Mark on the Wall
items.explanation: In his Socratic dialogue essay 'The Decay of Lying' (1889, collected in Intentions, 1891), Oscar Wilde's mouthpiece Vivian champions Aestheticism over nineteenth-century naturalism. Vivian declares that 'As a method, realism is a complete failure', arguing instead that Life imitates Art far more than Art imitates Life.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q31
items.stem:
Match the LIST-I with LIST-II
LIST-I (Writer) | LIST-II (Work)
A. D. G. Jones | I. Vertical Man / Horizontal World
B. Margaret Atwood | II. Patterns of Isolation: In English Canadian Fiction
C. John Moss | III. Survival
D. Laurence Ricou | IV. Butterfly on Rock
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In Canadian thematic literary criticism, D. G. Jones wrote Butterfly on a Rock (1970, A-IV), Margaret Atwood wrote Survival: A Thematic Guide to Canadian Literature (1972, B-III), John Moss wrote Patterns of Isolation in English Canadian Fiction (1974, C-II), and Laurence Ricou wrote Vertical Man/Horizontal World (1973, D-I).

items.title: Mock #03 · Q32
items.stem: Who along with Richard Hoggart and Stuart Hall was one of the founding figures of the school of thought now known as British Cultural Studies?
items.explanation: Welsh cultural critic and academic Raymond Williams—author of Culture and Society (1958) and The Long Revolution (1961)—was, alongside Richard Hoggart and Stuart Hall, a foundational intellectual pioneer of British Cultural Studies.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q33
items.stem:
Which of the following details about the Dramatis Personae of The Duchess of Malfi are correct?
A. FERDINAND [Duke of Calabria].
B. CARDINAL [Executioner].
C. ANTONIO [BOLOGNA, Steward of the Household to the Duchess].
D. DELIO [Court Officer].
E. DANIEL DE BOSOLA [Gentleman of the Horse to the Duchess].
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In the Dramatis Personae of John Webster's The Duchess of Malfi (1614), Ferdinand is the Duke of Calabria (A), Antonio Bologna is the Steward of the Household to the Duchess (C), and Daniel de Bosola is the Gentleman of the Horse to the Duchess (E).

items.title: Mock #03 · Q34
items.stem: Shakespeare's sonnets
options: are dedicated to an unknown "Mr. W.H."
are dedicated to James I of England
items.explanation: The 1609 quarto of Shake-speares Sonnets, published by Thomas Thorpe, bears a famous dedication to an unidentified 'Mr. W. H.' as 'the onlie begetter of these insuing sonnets', often conjectured to be William Herbert or Henry Wriothesley.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q35
items.stem:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of their publication :
(A) Jane Eyre
(B) Henry Esmond
(C) The Lady of the Last Minstrel
(D) Mary Barton
(E) Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
items.explanation: The chronological order of publication is Walter Scott's narrative poem The Lay of the Last Minstrel (1805), Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre (1847), Elizabeth Gaskell's Mary Barton (1848), William Makepeace Thackeray's Henry Esmond (1852), and Robert Louis Stevenson's Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886).

items.title: Mock #03 · Q36
items.stem: Who among the following American writers was the first Black American to become the U.S. Poet Laureate and Consultant in Poetry at the Library of Congress?
items.explanation: In 1993, Rita Francis Dove was named Poet Laureate Consultant in Poetry to the Library of Congress, becoming the first African American to hold the official title of United States Poet Laureate.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q37
items.stem:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Constantin Stanislavski collaborated with Anton Chekhov to stage dramas on stage.
Statement II: The book My Life in Art was written by Constantin Stanislavski.
In the light of the statements given above choose the correct answer given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true and Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false and Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both Statement I and Statement II are true: Russian theatre practitioner Constantin Stanislavski famously collaborated with Anton Chekhov to stage his major plays (including The Seagull, Uncle Vanya, Three Sisters, and The Cherry Orchard) at the Moscow Art Theatre, and Stanislavski wrote his autobiography My Life in Art (1924).

items.title: Mock #03 · Q38
items.stem: Andrew Marvell's "An Horatian Ode upon Cromwell's Return from Ireland" was written in
items.explanation: Andrew Marvell composed 'An Horatian Ode upon Cromwell's Return from Ireland' in the summer of 1650, immediately following Oliver Cromwell's return from his Irish campaign in May 1650 and before his invasion of Scotland.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q39
items.stem:
To which of the following theories New Historicism is indebted?
A. Marxism
B. Formalism
C. Reader-response Theory
D. Existentialism
E. Hermeneutics
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: New Historicism is theoretically indebted to Marxism (A) for its attention to power, ideology, and material history, and to Reader-Response Theory (C) for recognizing that both readers and critics interpret texts from within their own historical and cultural situatedness.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q40
items.stem: Identify the Fireside poets of the US.
options: T.S. Eliot, Wallace Stevens, William Carlos Williams
William Cullen Bryant, H.W. Longfellow, Oliver Wendell Holmes
Amy Lowell, Emily Dickinson, Phillis Wheatley
Marianne Moore, Elizabeth Bishop, Anne Seaton
items.explanation: The Fireside Poets were popular nineteenth-century New England poets: Bryant, Longfellow, Holmes, Whittier and Lowell.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q41
items.stem: Match List - I with List - II. List - I (Novel) List II (Subtitle) (A) The Castle of Otranto (I) A Pure Woman (B) Tess of the d'Urbervilles (II) The Modern Prometheus (C) Frankenstein (III) A Novel without A Hero (D) Vanity Fair (IV) A Gothic Story Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The correct novel-to-subtitle pairings are: Horace Walpole's The Castle of Otranto (1764) is subtitled A Gothic Story [(A)-(IV)]; Thomas Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891) is subtitled A Pure Woman: Faithfully Presented [(B)-(I)]; Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818) is subtitled The Modern Prometheus [(C)-(II)]; and W.M. Thackeray's Vanity Fair (1848) is subtitled A Novel without a Hero [(D)-(III)].

items.title: Mock #03 · Q42
items.stem:
Who among the following displays in her best ork the dual influence of feminism and
agic realism ?
items.explanation: British novelist Angela Carter is celebrated for masterfully blending socialist-feminist critique, psychoanalysis, and exuberant magic realism across postmodern fairy-tale revisions and carnivalesque novels such as The Bloody Chamber (1979) and Nights at the Circus (1984).

items.title: Mock #03 · Q43
items.meta: Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem: The term 'simulacra' in postmodern discourse is about: (A) Absence of vivid representation of reality (B) Artificially produced reality dubbed as authentic (C) A rejection of modernistic view of reality (D) The gap between the perception and reality (E) The psychological interplay at the level of subconscious Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In Simulacra and Simulation (1981), Jean Baudrillard defines simulacra as copies without an original - simulated realities that lack genuine referential substance (A) yet are produced and received as authentic in hyperreal consumer culture (B).

items.title: Mock #03 · Q44
items.stem:
As Sidney argues in A Defence of Poesy which discipline is more useful and praiseworthy
- history or poetry ?
options: Poetry where man can see "virtue exalted and vice punished" is more useful than history
History "being captivated to truth" is more useful than poetry
History is more useful for poetry is "an encouragement to unbridled wickedness
History and poetry are synonymous, and so both are useful
items.explanation: In An Apology for Poetry (A Defence of Poesy, 1595), Sir Philip Sidney argues that poetry is superior to history because the historian, tied to 'the particular truth of things', must often show the wicked prospering, whereas the poet creates a golden world where 'virtue is exalted and vice punished'.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q45
items.stem:
Arrange the chronological sequence in which the following works were published:

A. Reflections on the Revolution in France
B. Preface to Shakespeare
C. The Social Contract
D. Treatise on Human Nature
E. Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding

Choose the correct answer from the following options:
items.explanation: Eighteenth-century works in chronological order: David Hume's A Treatise of Human Nature (1739–40, D); Hume's An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748, E); Jean-Jacques Rousseau's The Social Contract (1762, C); Samuel Johnson's Preface to Shakespeare (1765, B); and Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790, A).

items.title: Mock #03 · Q46
items.stem: The Calcutta Chromosome (1995) is a novel exploring past and future. It has been written by:
items.explanation: The Calcutta Chromosome (1995) is an acclaimed science-fiction and speculative novel by Amitav Ghosh that intertwines Sir Ronald Ross's malaria discovery with subaltern counter-science, winning the Arthur C. Clarke Award in 1997.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q47
items.stem:
Assertion (A) :
 There is no unity or absolute source of the myth.
Reason (R) :
The focus or the source of the myth are always shadows and virtualities
which are elusive , unactualizable, and nonexistent in the first place. Any
search for the discursive unity in the myth is,  therefore, misplaced.
In the context of the above statements
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
items.explanation: Drawn from Jacques Derrida's 1966 essay 'Structure, Sign, and Play in the Discourse of the Human Sciences' (discussing Claude Lévi-Strauss), both statements are true and Reason (R) directly explains Assertion (A): because a myth has no fixed origin or centre, any quest for a totalizing discursive unity is misplaced.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q48
items.stem: Which one of the following observations of 'Lost Generation', a term coined by Gertrude Stein, is correct?
options: German Jews who survived the Second World War and went to Israel
The Irish Freedom fighters of the early Twentieth Century
The American expatriates in Europe after the First World War
items.explanation: Coined by Gertrude Stein and popularized by Ernest Hemingway as an epigraph to The Sun Also Rises (1926), the 'Lost Generation' refers to disillusioned American writers and expatriates living in Europe (especially Paris) after World War I.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q49
items.stem:
Which of the following books are written by Julia Kristeva?
A. Desire in Language: A Semiotic Approach to Literature and Art
B. Illuminations
C. Syntax and Semantics
D. La revolution du langage poétique
E. The Madwoman in the Attic
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Desire in Language: A Semiotic Approach to Literature and Art (1980, A) and La Révolution du langage poétique (Revolution in Poetic Language, 1974, D) were written by Bulgarian-French theorist Julia Kristeva. Illuminations is by Walter Benjamin, and The Madwoman in the Attic is by Sandra Gilbert and Susan Gubar.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q50
items.stem: David Malouf’s An Imaginary Life is a retelling of the story of :
items.explanation: Australian novelist David Malouf's lyrical novel An Imaginary Life (1978) retells the Roman poet Ovid's exile on the Black Sea coast at Tomis and his transformative spiritual relationship with a feral Child.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q51
items.stem: Match the character with the author : List – I I. Madeline II. Prometheus III. Urizen IV. Childe Harold List – II A. Blake B. Byron C. Shelley D. Keats
items.explanation: The correct pairings are: Madeline appears in John Keats's narrative poem The Eve of St. Agnes (1820) [I-D]; Prometheus is the suffering hero of Percy Bysshe Shelley's lyrical drama Prometheus Unbound (1820) [II-C]; Urizen is the embodiment of conventional reason and law in William Blake's The Book of Urizen (1794) [III-A]; and Childe Harold is the autobiographical wanderer in Lord Byron's Childe Harold's Pilgrimage (1812–1818) [IV-B].

items.title: Mock #03 · Q52
items.stem: Which of the following writers did NOT receive the Nobel Prize for Literature ?
items.explanation: Nigerian novelist Chinua Achebe (author of Things Fall Apart), though winner of the 2007 Man Booker International Prize, never received the Nobel Prize in Literature. Wole Soyinka (1986), Nadine Gordimer (1991), and J. M. Coetzee (2003) are all African Nobel laureates.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q53
items.stem:
Identify the two important works of Paul de Man from the following list :
(a)
Blindness and Insight
(b)
Allegories of Reading
(c)
Theoretical Essays
(d)
Criticism and Ideology
The right combination according to the code is
items.explanation: Blindness and Insight (1971) and Allegories of Reading (1979) are the two landmark books of deconstructive literary criticism by Yale School theorist Paul de Man. Theoretical Essays is by Fredric Jameson and Criticism and Ideology is by Terry Eagleton.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q54
items.stem: Who among the following is associated with the ideology of Utilitarianism ?
items.explanation: Nineteenth-century British philosopher and political economist John Stuart Mill (1806–1873) was the foremost exponent of Utilitarianism—the ethical doctrine of 'the greatest happiness of the greatest number' founded by Jeremy Bentham—which Mill refined in his treatise Utilitarianism (1861).

items.title: Mock #03 · Q55
items.stem:
Match the column:
(A) The moment of protagonist’s recognition in a narrative
(B) The decisive turn in tragedy by which the plot is resolved
(C) The inversion of an already established sequence
(D) The figure by which something distasteful is described in less repugnant terms
(I) Catastrophe
(II) Chiasmas
(IIl) Anagnorisis
(IV) Euphemism
items.explanation: In dramatic and literary terms, the protagonist's moment of recognition is Anagnorisis (A-III); the decisive resolving turn in tragedy is Catastrophe (B-I); the inverted sequence of terms (AB-BA) is Chiasmus (C-II); and substituting a mild expression for a harsh one is Euphemism (D-IV).

items.title: Mock #03 · Q56
items.stem: Who among the following is a well-known Neo-Aristotelian critic ?
items.explanation: Ronald Salmon (R. S.) Crane led the Chicago School of Neo-Aristotelian criticism and edited its manifesto Critics and Criticism: Ancient and Modern (1952), advocating a pluralistic, genre-based analysis of poetic plot and form against the verbal monism of the New Critics.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q57
items.stem:
Assertion (A) : A significant characteristic of modern British literature is the expression of an intense sense of uncertainty, disillusionment and despair.
Reason (R) : Because modern British writers have been deeply affected by the devastation of war and a feeling of disconnection from past traditions.
In the context of the two statements, which one of the following is correct ?
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
items.explanation: Modernist British literature is marked by pervasive uncertainty, fragmentation, and disillusionment (A), which directly stemmed from the trauma of the World Wars and the breakdown of Victorian religious, social, and cultural certainties (R).

items.title: Mock #03 · Q58
items.stem: Name the poet who has composed the following poems: (a) The Divine Image (b) The Holy Thursday (c) The Little Boy Lost (d) The Little Boy Found
items.explanation: All four poems were written and engraved by William Blake: 'The Divine Image', 'Holy Thursday', 'The Little Boy Lost', and 'The Little Boy Found' belong to his illuminated masterwork Songs of Innocence (1789), paired with companion poems in Songs of Experience (1794).

items.title: Mock #03 · Q59
items.stem:
According to Gerard Genette, which of the following are types of narrators?
A. Extradiegetic
B. Heterodiegetic
C. Intradiegetic
D. Homodiegetic
E. Interdiegetic

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In Narrative Discourse (1972), Gérard Genette classifies narrators by narrative level into extradiegetic (A) and intradiegetic (C), and by relationship to the story into heterodiegetic (B) and homodiegetic (D); only 'interdiegetic' (E) is not a Genette term, so NTA accepted Options 1, 2, and 3.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q60
items.stem: In Women in Love what is Winifred's pekinese dog called ?
items.explanation: In D. H. Lawrence's novel Women in Love (1920), young Winifred Crich has a pampered Pekingese dog named Looloo, while her fierce pet rabbit—featured in a famous chapter—is named Bismarck.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q61
items.stem:

A. Epigram
B. Epigone
C. Diegesis
D. Elision

List II (Definition):
I. An inferior or derivative follower of a more distinguished writer
II. The slurring or suppression of a vowel sound or syllable
III. A short poem with a witty turn of thought or a wittily condensed expression in prose.
IV. A term used in modern narratology to designate the narrated events as a level distinct from that of the narration.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The literary terms match their definitions as follows: an Epigram is a short poem with a witty turn of thought or condensed prose expression (A-III), an Epigone is an inferior or derivative follower of a distinguished writer (B-I), Diegesis designates the narrated story-world distinct from the level of narration (C-IV), and Elision is the slurring or suppression of a vowel sound or syllable (D-II).

items.title: Mock #03 · Q62

associated with the early plays of
items.explanation: Coined by drama critic Irving Wardle in 1958, 'comedy of menace' describes the early plays of Harold Pinter—such as The Room (1957), The Birthday Party (1958), and The Dumb Waiter (1957)—in which ordinary comic dialogue is underscored by vague, looming terror and intimidation.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q63
items.stem:

A. John of Trevisa
B. Julian of Norwich
C. John Mandeville
D. Bernard of Clairvaux
E. Walter Hilton

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In 14th-century Middle English literature, John of Trevisa (translator of Ranulf Higden's Polychronicon) and the author of The Travels of Sir John Mandeville composed secular prose, whereas Julian of Norwich and Walter Hilton were Christian devotional mystics, and Bernard of Clairvaux lived in the 12th century.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q64
items.stem: Which one of the following statements is true about Aristotle's poetics?
options: He asserted the value of poetry by focusing on imitation (mimesis) rather than rhetoric
He asserted the value of poetry by focusing on both rhetoric and imitation (mimesis)
He asserted the value of poetry by giving preference to rhetoric over imitation (mimesis)
He asserted the value of poetry by integrating rhetoric and imitation (mimesis)
items.explanation: In his treatise Poetics, Aristotle defines poetry and drama fundamentally as modes of imitation (mimesis) that represent human action and universal truths, whereas he treats persuasive speech separately in his Rhetoric. By grounding poetry in mimesis and catharsis, Aristotle defended its philosophical and moral value against Plato's critique.

coined by

items.title: Mock #03 · Q70
items.stem: No, no thou hast not felt the lapse of hours ! For what wears out the life of mortal men ? 'Tis that repeated shocks, again, again, Exhaust the energy of strongest souls And numb the elastic powers … Who does the poet address here ?
items.explanation: These lines are from Matthew Arnold's pastoral elegy 'The Scholar-Gipsy' (1853). The speaker addresses the legendary seventeenth-century Oxford scholar who joined a band of gypsies, contrasting his ageless, single-minded quest with the exhausting 'sick hurry and divided aims' of modern Victorian life.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q71
items.stem:
Which two of the following strictly follow the parameters of documentation prescribed by the
eighth edition of the MLA Handbook?

A. Nunberg, Geoffrey, editor. The Future of the Book. U of California P, 1996.

B. Puig, Manuel. Kiss of the Spider Woman. Trans. Thomas Colchie, London: Vintage, 1991.

C. Nunberg, Geoffrey, ed. The Future of the Book. Berkeley: U of California P, 1996.

D. Puig, Manuel. Kiss of the Spider Woman. Translated by Thomas Colchie, Vintage Books, 1991.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: The eighth edition of the MLA Handbook (2016) streamlined bibliographic citations by eliminating the city of publication and replacing traditional Latinate abbreviations like 'ed.' and 'Trans.' with spelled-out roles ('editor' and 'Translated by'). Entries A and D strictly follow these eighth-edition rules, whereas B and C use older seventh-edition conventions.

W.H. Anden in his oxford lectures on poetry

items.title: Mock #03 · Q75
items.stem:
Which of the following are features of the 'Theatre of the Absurd'?
A. emphasis on the central role of God in the universe

B. presentation of futile actions devoid of any goal
C. portrayal of situations that point to the meaningfulness of life
D. lacking in conflicts and dramatic tensions
E. presenting players in a stasis or drift without definite roles
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Coined by Martin Esslin in 1961, the Theatre of the Absurd presents purposeless, repetitive actions in a world devoid of divine meaning (B), abandons conventional plot conflict and dramatic resolution (D), and depicts characters trapped in existential stasis (E), making B, D and E correct.

items.explanation: J. D. Scott, literary editor of The Spectator, coined the term 'The Movement' in an anonymous October 1954 article ('In the Movement') to describe the anti-Romantic, ironic postwar British writers including Philip Larkin, Kingsley Amis, and Donald Davie.

items.explanation: The characters match Ben Jonson's comedies as follows: Knowell (Knowles) is the suspicious father in Everyman in His Humour (1598) [I-C]; Bonario is the honorable young heir in Volpone (1606) [II-A]; Morose is the misanthropic bachelor who hates noise in Epicoene (1609) [III-D]; and Subtle is the titular fraudulent charlatan in The Alchemist (1610) [IV-B].

items.title: Mock #03 · Q91
items.stem:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below :
Some have maintained that a stable and tranquil state of health is not really a pleasure, on the grounds that the presence of health cannot be felt except through external stimulus. The Utopians (who have considered the matter thoroughly) long ago rejected this opinion. On the contrary, they nearly all agree that health is crucial to pleasure. Since pain is inherent in diseases, they argue, and pain is the bitter enemy of pleasure, just as disease is the enemy of health, then pleasure must be inherent in quiet good health. You may say pain is not the disease itself, simply an accompanying effect; but they argue that that makes no difference since the effect is the same either way. For whether health is itself a pleasure or is merely the cause of pleasure (as fire is the cause of heat), the fact remains that those who have stable health must also have pleasure.

What does the first line of the passage say about external stimulus ?
options: External stimulus is the by-product of health
External stimulus is irrelevant to the experience of health
External stimulus is necessary condition for the experience of health
items.explanation: The opening line of the passage from Thomas More's Utopia states that the Utopians debate whether health can be felt without some external stimulus, arguing that an external stimulus is a necessary condition for experiencing the sensation of bodily health.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q96
items.meta: Unit IV / Unit VIII: Prose & Criticism
items.stem:
Read the following passage/poetry carefully and answer the questions given below :
Between my finger and my thumb
The squat pen rests; Snug as a gun.
Under my window, a clean rasping sound:
When the spade sinks into gravelly ground
My father, digging. I look down
Till his straining rump among the flower beds
Bends low, comes up twenty years away
Stooping in rhythm through potato drills
Where he was digging.
The coarse boot nested on the leg, the shaft
Against the inside knee was levered firmly.
He rooted out tall tops, buried the bright edge deep
To scatter new potatoes that we picked,
Loving their cool hardness in our hands.

The comparison of gun to a pen in the poem signifies :
options: the power of written word to bring about change
that the act of writing can be as lethal as using a weapon
the high admiration of the speaker about father's ability to use both pen and spade
items.explanation: In the opening lines of Seamus Heaney's 'Digging' ('Between my finger and my thumb / The squat pen rests; snug as a gun'), the simile comparing the pen to a gun signifies that the act of writing carries a potent, lethal force comparable to a weapon.

What is the nature of the setting in the poem ?
options: The setting is industrial yet solitary
The setting is urban and noisy
The setting is rural and serene
The setting is suburban and bustling
items.explanation: The poem is set in the quiet Irish countryside of flower beds, gravelly ground, and potato drills, creating a rural and serene setting.

items.title: Mock #03 · Q99
items.meta: Unit IV / Unit VIII: Prose & Criticism
items.stem:
Read the following passage/poetry carefully and answer the questions given below :
Between my finger and my thumb
The squat pen rests; Snug as a gun.
Under my window, a clean rasping sound:
When the spade sinks into gravelly ground
My father, digging. I look down
Till his straining rump among the flower beds
Bends low, comes up twenty years away
Stooping in rhythm through potato drills
Where he was digging.
The coarse boot nested on the leg, the shaft
Against the inside knee was levered firmly.
He rooted out tall tops, buried the bright edge deep
To scatter new potatoes that we picked,
Loving their cool hardness in our hands.

In the line "when the spade sinks into gravelly ground" which figure of speech has been used ?
items.explanation: The line 'When the spade sinks into gravelly ground' repeats the initial consonant sounds /s/ ('spade sinks') and /g/ ('gravelly ground'), which is a clear example of alliteration.

The physical and mental work need to be treated at an equal level
Poetry has done no good for the making of a better world
